units.text: Water reaching the saturated zone can contribute to groundwater recharge, but not all infiltrating water reaches that zone. Groundwater fills pores or fractures in saturated material. An aquifer is a geologic formation that stores and transmits usable quantities of groundwater. Groundwater can move through connected openings and discharge into streams, lakes, or springs. A spring occurs where groundwater emerges at the surface. These connections allow groundwater to maintain flow in some streams during dry periods, linking underground storage to visible surface water.

units.text: Storage and movement occur over different timescales, so water does not follow one compulsory loop. A water budget compares inputs, outputs, and changes in storage within a defined area and time interval. Human activities can alter this balance. Paved surfaces often reduce infiltration and increase rapid runoff. Pumping removes groundwater, and sustained withdrawals greater than replenishment can reduce groundwater storage. Understanding these pathways helps explain how rainfall, underground reserves, and downstream water availability are connected.
